summary: Extends DHCPv4 leasequery (RFC 4388) so a relay agent can look up lease information by remote ID, not only by data it already has. This is useful when the relay agent has lost its stored lease information. It updates RFC 4388 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A helper that forgot who has which address can ask the address server and find the answer using the name of the connection.

questions: what is dhcp lease query by remote id
why does a relay agent need lease query
subtitle: Lets a relay agent that lost its memory ask a DHCP server for every lease on a circuit, using the circuit's Remote ID.

tldr.problem: A DHCP relay agent that reboots loses the lease information it had gleaned. The existing lease query types of RFC 4388 only work when a client sends data, which causes outages, heavy negative caching and slow-path anti-spoofing.
tldr.mechanism: A new query type sends a DHCPLEASEQUERY carrying only a Remote ID sub-option of the Relay Agent Information option. The server answers DHCPLEASEACTIVE with the associated addresses, or DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN.
tldr.outcome: The relay agent can rebuild all lease information for a connection before clients send upstream traffic. The query reveals consolidated lease data, so the RFC says authentication such as RFC 3118 is critical.

today: RFC 6148 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2011. It updates RFC 4388 and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Query by Remote ID
sections.content:
DHCP relay agents watch DHCP messages and add a Relay Agent Information option before passing them on. Some also glean lease information from the server's replies, using it to block spoofing by clients and sometimes to install routing information. A reboot loses that information.

RFC 4388 lets a relay agent recover leases from the server, but its query types are data-driven: the agent queries only after a client sends data, by source MAC or IP address. With thousands of clients that does not scale, does not give a consolidated view of a circuit, and forces the agent to spend resources on negative caching, especially under spoofing attacks.

The motivating example is a DSLAM acting as relay agent. After a reboot it should query for all connections, and one DSL circuit can have several clients behind it.
sections.eli5: If the helper only asks about a house when someone knocks, it takes a long time and lots of notes. It is better to ask for the whole street list right away.

sections.title: Fast Path and Slow Path
sections.content:
Most networking boxes have a fast path, where a network processor or ASIC forwards data at very high speed, and a slow path, the control plane, with very limited buffers. Regular forwarding should stay in the fast path. Slow path work can become a bottleneck.

An access concentrator wants anti-spoofing to happen in the fast path, with one list of the IP addresses assigned by DHCP servers and all other upstream traffic dropped. The data-driven query types of RFC 4388 give increased outage time for clients, excessive negative caching under attack, and anti-spoofing in the slow path. The RFC says a new mechanism is needed.
sections.eli5: A busy post office has a fast conveyor belt and a slow desk. Checking every parcel at the slow desk jams things up, so the checking list should be ready before the parcels arrive.

sections.title: The Query Message
sections.content:
RFC 3046 defines the Circuit ID (sub-option 1, unique to the relay agent) and the Remote ID (sub-option 2, globally unique in the network and configured per circuit or connection). Because the Remote ID is normally pre-provisioned, it survives a reboot. The access concentrator sends one lease query by Remote ID for each connection when it comes up.

The DHCPLEASEQUERY uses the format of RFC 2131 with message type 10 in option 53. It MUST contain option 82 with only a Remote ID sub-option. The Parameter Request List MUST include the Associated-IP option code. ciaddr MUST be zero, htype, hlen and chaddr MUST be zero, and the Client Identifier option (61) MUST NOT appear.

The query SHOULD go to a server known to hold authoritative data for the Remote ID. Without that knowledge it SHOULD be sent to all DHCP servers configured for the relay agent, if known.
sections.eli5: The question carries just one label: the name of the connection. Everything else on the form is left blank on purpose.

sections.title: How the Server Answers
sections.content:
The server MUST reply DHCPLEASEACTIVE if there is an active lease for the Remote ID, and otherwise MUST reply DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN. A server that does not implement this query type SHOULD simply not respond. Replies are unicast to the address in the query's giaddr field.

In an active reply, ciaddr MUST hold the address with the latest client-last-transaction-time for the client behind that Remote ID, unless the administrator configured another preference. If more than one address was involved, all of them MUST be listed in the Associated-IP option, even if it was not requested, which keeps compatibility with RFC 4388. An unknown reply MUST echo option 82 and include no other option.
sections.eli5: The server says 'yes, here is who lives there' with the newest address first, or 'I do not know that connection'.

sections.title: What the Relay Agent Does Next
sections.content:
On DHCPLEASEACTIVE, the access concentrator SHOULD use htype, hlen, chaddr and the Relay Agent Information option to refresh its location information for that address. It is likely to then query by IP address for each address in the Associated-IP option.

On DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN, the server has no definitive information. The agent MAY store this, but SHOULD NOT send another query with the same Remote ID to the same server. Because a Remote ID query returns complete information for everything behind the connection, negative caching has far less impact and periodic re-queries caused by DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN are removed. A missing response is handled as in RFC 4388, as is use of multiple servers. As an implementation note, a server should index its lease bindings by Remote ID to answer efficiently.
sections.eli5: After getting the list, the helper writes down each address and who owns it. If the answer was 'unknown', it does not keep asking the same question.

sections.title: Compatibility with RFC 4388
sections.content:
The extension is compatible with RFC 4388 implementations. A client with this extension can work with a server without it by using the older query types, and a server with it can serve clients that lack it.

Two points need care. A query by IP address, MAC address or Client Identifier that happens to include option 82 with a Remote ID is still treated as that older query type. And while RFC 4388 says a DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN must have no other option, a reply to a Remote ID query MUST include option 82.
sections.eli5: New and old helpers can still work together, with one small change to how the 'unknown' answer is written.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document inherits the security concerns of RFC 4388 and adds one: a Remote ID query makes the server return consolidated lease-binding information. If done from an unauthorized source, this may leak that information.

The RFC states that it is critical to deploy the authentication techniques of RFC 3118 to prevent unauthorized lease queries.
sections.eli5: The list shows who lives where, so only the real helper should be allowed to ask for it.
